subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The Cosmic Microwave Background
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Cosmic Microwave Background.

hook.text: In 1965, two radio engineers found mysterious static in their antenna. It came from every direction equally.

buildup.text: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson couldn't eliminate the noise. They even removed pigeon droppings from the dish.

discovery.text: The static was the Cosmic Microwave Background—the afterglow of the Big Bang, cooled to just 2.7 degrees above absolute zero.

twist.text: They won the 1978 Nobel Prize for a discovery they stumbled upon by accident while doing unrelated work.

climax.text: The CMB is the strongest evidence for the Big Bang. It matches predictions to extraordinary precision.

punchline.text: Pigeon poop couldn't explain it. It was the glow of creation.

quiz.question: How was the Cosmic Microwave Background discovered?
options: Accidentally, by two radio engineers who couldn't eliminate mysterious static
Deliberately, by a space telescope designed to detect it
Through mathematical predictions that were later confirmed

details.summary: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is the faint glow of radiation left over from when the universe cooled enough for atoms to form, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
details.whyItMatters: The CMB is the oldest light in the universe — a direct snapshot of conditions 380,000 years after the Big Bang. Its temperature variations map the density fluctuations that grew into galaxies, galaxy clusters, and the cosmic web.
takeaways: The CMB is leftover radiation from 380,000 years after the Big Bang
It fills the entire sky at a uniform temperature of 2.7 Kelvin
Tiny fluctuations reveal the seeds of all cosmic structure

faq.question: How was the cosmic microwave background discovered?
faq.answer: In 1965, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs detected persistent microwave static they couldn't eliminate. Cosmologists at Princeton recognized it as the predicted thermal echo of the Big Bang. Penzias and Wilson won the 1978 Nobel Prize for this accidental discovery.

faq.question: What do the CMB fluctuations tell us?
faq.answer: The pattern of temperature variations reveals the universe's geometry (flat), age (13.8 billion years), composition (5% normal matter, 27% dark matter, 68% dark energy), and expansion rate. The CMB is cosmology's most information-rich observable, constraining virtually all cosmological parameters.
